item.title: Impact of MRSA nasal PCR in the emergency department on duration of vancomycin and linezolid for pneumonia
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Introduction: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is a common cause of nosocomial pneumonia, often prompting empiric anti-MRSA therapy despite low prevalence in emergency department (ED) presentations. MRSA nasal polymerase chain reaction (PCR) offers a rapid, non-invasive method to guide de-escalation of MRSA-targeted therapy. This study aims to evaluate the impact of pharmacist-driven MRSA nasal PCR ordering in the ED on the duration of anti-MRSA therapy.

Methods: We conducted a quasi-experimental non-equivalent control study at a single academic center using data from an electronic health record. Adult ED patients with suspected pneumonia who received anti-MRSA therapy in the ED and were subsequently admitted were included. Emergency department pharmacists were responsible for ordering MRSA nasal PCR in compliance with a pre-existing hospital protocol. ED nurses facilitated MRSA nasal PCR collection in the ED.

Results: A total of 200 patients were included in the final analysis. The median duration of anti-MRSA therapy was 5.90 h and 1.13 h for pre- and post-intervention groups, respectively (p = 0.006). Incidence of MRSA nasal PCRs ordered increased from 69.4% pre-intervention to 86.3% post-intervention (p = 0.18). Median length of hospital stay was not significantly different between groups (5.0 days vs. 6.0 days, p = 0.10).

Conclusions: Pharmacist-driven MRSA nasal PCR ordering in the ED significantly reduced anti-MRSA therapy duration without adversely affecting 30-day readmission rates or all-cause 30-day mortality. These findings highlight the value of pharmacist engagement in antibiotic stewardship in the ED.

Skaar SM, Wex N, Wehling H, O'Driscoll T, Dang CH

item.title: Administered opioids and benzodiazepines and the interpretation of positive trauma urine drug screens
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Background: Urine drug screening (UDS) is routine in trauma care, and results populate trauma registries, quality review, and research. Trauma patients receive opioids and benzodiazepines before urine is collected, so a positive class-matched screen may reflect administered drug rather than pre-injury use. We estimated the magnitude of this effect by drug class and its impact on reported prevalence.

Methods: Retrospective cohort of all trauma patients at a Level II center, 2023-2024 (n = 2538), of whom 1420 (55.9%) underwent UDS. Medication administration was matched to the corresponding immunoassay channel, with fentanyl analyzed against its dedicated assay and opiate-assay-matched opioid against the opiate assay. Logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, Injury Severity Score, activation, intubation, and substance use disorder. Treatment-associated positives were estimated by g-computation with bootstrap confidence intervals; cannabinoids, amphetamines, and cocaine were negative controls.

Results: Class-matched positivity greatly exceeded unexposed positivity: 70.0% versus 12.5% for the fentanyl assay (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 15.3, 95% CI 11.5-20.4), 59.0% versus 19.0% for the opiate assay given an opiate-assay-matched opioid (aOR 5.9), and 51.6% versus 8.9% for benzodiazepines (aOR 6.1). Restricting exposure to pre-hospital administration, which necessarily precedes collection, preserved the effect (fentanyl aOR 19.9). Negative controls showed minimal association (amphetamine aOR 1.1). By g-computation, an estimated 62.8% (56.9-68.6) of fentanyl-assay positives, 33.7% of opiate positives, and 29.3% of benzodiazepine positives were associated with administered drug. Any-positive prevalence was 64.4% overall and 37.3% among patients given neither class.

Conclusions: Administered fentanyl was associated with a model-estimated majority of positive fentanyl-assay screens; administered opiates and benzodiazepines were associated with smaller shares of their corresponding positive screens. Class-matched results should be interpreted alongside the medication record. These findings do not establish the source or analytical validity of an individual positive result.

Potts C, Ali A, Gandhi S, Ghafoor M, May D

item.title: Association between mechanical ventilation with positive end-expiratory pressure and outcomes in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Aim: The effect of positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) during intermittent positive pressure ventilation in patients undergoing cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) on outcome is unknown. The aim of this study was to evaluate the association between the use of PEEP during cardiopulmonary resuscitation and clinical outcomes in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) patients.

Methods: We conducted a single-centre observational cohort study using a retrospective analysis of data collected prospectively within a dedicated research registry of adult OHCA patients managed by a physician-staffed prehospital emergency medical team. All included patients were intubated and ventilated either with mechanical ventilation using PEEP or with manual ventilation without PEEP. Intratracheal pressure was continuously recorded via a catheter connected to a portable device, allowing objective verification of PEEP application and ventilation rate. The association between mechanical ventilation with PEEP use and clinical outcomes was evaluated using multivariable logistic regression adjusted for relevant confounders.

Results: 362 patients were included, with a median age of 65 years (54-79), of whom 250 (69.1%) were male. Median ventilation rate was 15 breaths/min (10-19). Of all patients, 149 (41.2%) achieved Return Of Spontaneous Circulation (ROSC) and 31 (8.6%) survived to hospital discharge. The adjusted odds ratio (OR) of mechanical ventilation with PEEP for achieving ROSC was 1.58 (95% CI 1.01-2.50, p = 0.048). The unadjusted OR of mechanical ventilation with PEEP for survival to hospital discharge was 2.22 (95% CI 1.03-4.78; p = 0.037).

Conclusion: The use of mechanical ventilation with PEEP during CPR in OHCA patients was associated with higher likelihood of ROSC.

item.title: Tachycardia and rhabdomyolysis after use of melanotan and an uncommon synthetic cannabinoid receptor agonist
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Various medicinal and non-medicinal substances are available on the internet for a variety of intended effects such as recreational use, performance enhancement, and modification of body appearance. Melanotans are synthetic agonists of melanocyte stimulating hormone (a-MSH) used to promote tanning. We describe a young adult male presenting to the ED with tachycardia and tremors reportedly following melanotan injection. Clinical suspicion and laboratory confirmation led to detection of an undisclosed synthetic cannabinoid receptor agonist (SCRA) seldom reported in the US. We discuss the likely contributions of both substances to the findings in this case.

item.title: A retrospective assessment of intubation prior to burn center arrival
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Background: Pre-burn center intubation is frequently performed in burn patients with suspected inhalation injury because of concern for progressive airway edema. However, contemporary studies suggest that many of these intubations may be unnecessary. We evaluated factors associated with prolonged mechanical ventilation following pre-burn center intubation in burn-injured patients.

Methods: We performed a retrospective cohort study of burn patients admitted to a single regional burn center from July 1, 2015, to June 30, 2023 who were intubated in the field or at referring facilities prior to arrival. Patients intubated through tracheostomy were excluded. Patients were stratified by duration of post-admission mechanical ventilation. Demographics, burn characteristics, inhalation injury findings, and documented intubation criteria were analyzed. Multivariate logistic regression identified factors associated with prolonged ventilation.

Results: Among 306 patients who met inclusion criteria, 147 (48%) were extubated within 24 h of admission. Patients requiring over 24 h of ventilation had larger burns, more inhalation injuries, longer hospital length of stay, and higher rates of ventilator-associated pneumonia and sepsis. Traditional findings such as singed facial hair, soot in the oropharynx, and suspected smoke inhalation poorly discriminated prolonged ventilator needs. Multivariate analysis demonstrated that indoor fire mechanism (OR 1.98, p = 0.004), signs of respiratory distress (OR 1.98, p = 0.008), and anticipated transfer of a patient with major burn without qualified medical professional to intubate en route (OR 2.69, p < 0.001) were associated with longer ventilation.

Conclusions: Our data suggests that physiology-based indicators of respiratory compromise may be more effective than traditional physical exam findings in optimizing airway management strategies before transfer to a burn center.

item.title: Ultrasound-guided hydrodissection for anterior cutaneous nerve entrapment syndrome: A case series
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Anterior cutaneous nerve entrapment syndrome (ACNES) is an uncommon, non-emergent cause of chronic abdominal wall pain arising from entrapment of the terminal branches of the T7-T12 intercostal nerves at the anterior rectus sheath. It is usually recognized only after laboratory and imaging studies have excluded intra-abdominal causes, often after repeated evaluations. Prior abdominal surgery is a recognized risk factor due to fascial scarring. Ultrasound-guided hydrodissection with 5% dextrose in water (D5W) and dilute lidocaine has been described in case reports as a minimally invasive treatment that may relieve pain and release the entrapped nerve. We present two patients who developed post-surgical ACNES following laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and laparoscopic cholecystectomy, respectively. Each presented to the ED with severe abdominal wall pain (NRS 9/10 and 10/10) and negative intra-abdominal workup. Both patients met diagnostic criteria including positive Carnett's sign, positive pinch test, and >90% pain reduction after ultrasound-guided hydrodissection. On chart review, pain relief was sustained at 6 weeks (Case 1) and 4 weeks (Case 2), and neither patient received other treatment after discharge. In these selected patients, bedside ultrasound-guided hydrodissection was feasible and was followed by rapid pain relief. Prospective, comparative studies are needed to establish its place within the ACNES treatment algorithm and to assess durability beyond the short-term follow-up reported here.

item.title: Secure chat and critical/urgent imaging-result communication in a multisite emergency department system
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Background: Closed-loop communication of critical and urgent imaging findings is essential for patient safety, but traditional verbal-only workflows can introduce friction and limit communication throughput. Epic Secure Chat, an EHR-integrated messaging platform, may reduce friction while preserving closed-loop communication requirements. This study evaluated communication volume, radiologist interpretation throughput, clinician experience, and reported safety events following implementation of a Secure Chat-first protocol.

Methods: A prospective pre-post cohort study of operational outcomes was conducted across 26 emergency departments within a large academic health system, with a concurrent post-implementation survey. Following a 205-day overnight Secure Chat pilot, operational data were compared with a 161-day pre-implementation period using paired t-tests. Communication and examination volumes were normalized by time period. Linear regression was used to assess the association between Secure Chat volume and interpretation throughput change.

Results: Survey responses were obtained from 48 emergency physicians (20.2%) and 19 radiologists (48.7%). Most emergency physicians (77%) and radiologists (95%) supported Secure Chat as a supplemental modality and reported improved communication ease. Documented critical and urgent result communications increased by 26.5% (mean increase 21.4 communications per radiologist; 95% CI 2.9-39.8; p=0.026). Radiologist interpretation throughput did not significantly change (+0.58%; p=0.833), with no association between Secure Chat volume and throughput change (R2=0.023; p=0.508). No Secure Chat-associated safety events were identified across 1087 reviewed communications.

Conclusion: Implementation of a Secure Chat-first protocol with a verbal failsafe was associated with increased communication volume without a reduction in radiologist throughput or identified safety events.

Prior presentations: American College of Emergency Physicians National Meeting, Salt Lake City, Utah 2025.

Simon EL, Mann W, Baskin B, Mody R, Meldon S

item.title: Impact of the provider-in-triage model on computed tomography and ultrasound imaging in renal colic
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Introduction: Physician-in-Triage (PIT) models may influence diagnostic imaging decisions in the emergency department (ED). We evaluated the association between PIT exposure and imaging utilization among patients with renal colic and examined the influence of physician ultrasound training on imaging selection.

Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults with an ED diagnosis of renal colic at a single tertiary ED from January 2024 through December 2025. A prespecified lower-risk subgroup included patients aged <51 years with prior nephrolithiasis, no infection, and normal creatinine. The primary exposure was PIT evaluation. Outcomes included computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis (CTAP), point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS), and radiology-performed renal ultrasound (RUS) utilization. Multivariable logistic regression was used to evaluate the association between PIT exposure and each imaging outcome after adjustment for age, gender, emergency severity index, admission, and race.

Results: Of 1041 patients, 596 (57.3%) were exposed to PIT. CTAP utilization was higher among PIT-exposed patients than non-PIT patients (72.9% vs 66.1%; adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.40, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.07-1.85). PIT exposure was associated with lower POCUS utilization (10.3% vs 18.6%; aOR 0.49, 95% CI 0.34-0.70), while RUS utilization was similar (10.1% vs 9.0%; aOR 1.17, 95% CI 0.76-1.79). Overall ultrasound utilization (POCUS or RUS) was also lower among PIT-exposed patients (20.1% vs 26.7%; aOR 0.69, 95% CI 0.51-0.93). In the lower-risk subgroup, PIT exposure remained associated with greater CTAP utilization (63.6% vs 48.1%, p = 0.028) and lower POCUS utilization (14.4% vs 30.4%, p = 0.008). Ultrasound-trained attendings used CTAP less frequently than non-ultrasound-trained attendings (57.8% vs 71.8%; aOR for non-ultrasound-trained physicians 1.86, 95% CI 1.18-2.93).

Conclusion: PIT exposure was associated with greater CTAP and lower ultrasound utilization in patients with renal colic, including among a prespecified lower-risk cohort. Ultrasound-trained physicians used ultrasound more frequently and CTAP less frequently in renal colic patients.

Thom C, Mullins C, Spirek B, Moak J

item.title: Diagnostic accuracy of serum procalcitonin for pneumonia in patients with acute dyspnea: a systematic review and meta-analysis
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Background: Several studies have investigated the diagnostic value of serum procalcitonin (PCT) for pneumonia in patients with acute dyspnea, but results have been inconsistent. This systematic review aimed to determine the diagnostic accuracy of serum PCT for pneumonia in patients with acute dyspnea.

Methods: We searched the PubMed and Web of Science databases to identify studies evaluating the diagnostic accuracy of serum PCT for pneumonia-associated acute dyspnea published before October 1, 2025. The quality of the included studies was assessed using the revised Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies (QUADAS-2). We used a bivariate model to be pooled sensitivity and specificity. The overall diagnostic accuracy was evaluated using a summary receiver operating characteristic curve (sROC). Deek's test was used to assess publication bias.

Results: We included 6 studies involving 2341 patients (576 with pneumonia and 1765 without). Serum PCT's pooled sensitivity and specificity for diagnosing pneumonia-related acute dyspnea were 0.67 (95% CI: 0.58-0.75) and 0.76 (95% CI: 0.67-0.83), respectively. The area under the sROC curve (AUC) was 0.77 (95% CI: 0.73-0.80). The positive likelihood ratio (PLR) and negative likelihood ratio (NLR) were 2.8 (95% CI: 2.0-3.8) and 0.44 (95% CI: 0.34-0.56), respectively. The diagnostic odds ratio (DOR) was 6 (95% CI: 4-10). The included studies showed no significant publication bias.

Conclusions: Serum PCT has only moderate diagnostic value for pneumonia-related acute dyspnea and is insufficient to confirm or exclude pneumonia when used alone.

Cui JY, Wang HJ, Xu YN, Wen JX, Hou WJ, Hao XL
